set.approach: There is no trail to Mount Fairchild itself, but the standard approach follows a well-defined maintained-trail corridor before turning to off-trail wilderness travel. Start at the Sol Duc River Trailhead (end of Sol Duc Road) on the Sol Duc River Trail. At 0.8 mi pass Sol Duc Falls, and at 0.9 mi reach the Lovers Lane junction; branch left onto the Deer Lake Trail, which climbs steeply and relentlessly through switchbacks to Deer Lake (3.4 mi, ~3,527 ft) — the first reliable water and the last easy camping before things get serious. Beyond Deer Lake the trail continues up through Potholes Meadows (~5 mi) and gains the High Divide ridge crest around 6 mi/4,730 ft, with good views and intermittent tarns/snowmelt for water. At 7.4 mi pass the Seven Lakes Basin junction (4,900 ft) — a good last water/camp option — then continue along High Divide past or near Bogachiel Peak (5,474 ft). At roughly 10.2 mi, leave the maintained trail system at the Cat Basin junction; from here it is off-trail cross-country and boot-path travel only, dropping into Cat Basin below Cat Peak (5,940 ft) and then climbing/sidehilling toward Mount Carrie (6,995 ft). Many parties use the exposed, loose-talus sidehill traverse across Carrie's south face known as "the Catwalk"; an alternative preferred by some climbers is to stay higher on Carrie's north side, which avoids the worst sidehilling and leads up Carrie's ridge and upper flanks to its summit. The route to Fairchild starts from Mount Carrie's summit: head northeast down the Carrie Glacier (rope up and put on crampons here; ice axe mandatory most of the season), circle around to the north of Fairchild, and climb its Southwest Ridge to the 6,899 ft summit. This final section is only thinly described, so expect to find the line yourself. One-way distance to this point is roughly 12 miles with substantial cumulative gain from repeated up-and-down over Bogachiel Peak, Cat Peak, and the Carrie ridge system, consistent with the ~8,000 ft round-trip gain. Hazards: early-season creek crossings near Sol Duc Falls, steep loose-scree switchbacks on the Deer Lake Trail, serious exposure and loose rock on the Catwalk traverse, crevasses and snow bridges on the Carrie Glacier requiring roped glacier travel (especially early/mid-summer), no reliable water between Cat Basin and the glacier, and heavy route-finding demands in fog/whiteout since the entire Cat Basin-to-summit section is unmarked wilderness travel.
set.descent_text: This is a walk-off/glacier-descent route with no rappelling. Descend by reversing the ascent line: from the summit, descend the Southwest Ridge, circle back around the north side of the peak and reclimb the Carrie Glacier roped up with crampons to Mount Carrie's summit, then descend Mount Carrie's north-side ridge. Sidehill/traverse back across the Catwalk (or the north-side alternative) to Cat Basin, drop to rejoin the maintained High Divide Trail at the Cat Basin junction (~10.2 mi mark), and retrace the trail past the Seven Lakes Basin junction, Bogachiel Peak, Potholes Meadows, Deer Lake, and Lovers Lane back down to Sol Duc Falls and the Sol Duc River Trailhead. Some parties instead continue the descent onward as part of the broader Bailey Range Traverse — dropping south past Ruth Peak toward Stephen Lake/Queets Basin and exiting via the Elwha (Whiskey Bend) or Hoh River trailheads — but that is a different, longer one-way multi-day itinerary rather than the out-and-back standard route matching this route's distance and gain. Descent hazards mirror the approach: crevasse fall potential on the glacier (softening snow in the afternoon raises post-holing/slot risk, so an early turnaround is wise), loose talus on the Carrie sidehill, fatigue-driven route-finding errors in the featureless heather and scree of Cat Basin, and long, tired-legs reversal of the steep Deer Lake Trail switchbacks.
set.beta: Mount Fairchild is the second-highest peak in the Bailey Range and is accessed via two primary routes: (1) the High Divide approach via Sol Duc and Mount Carrie, or (2) from the Elwha River over Mount Fitzhenry. Both routes involve significant glacier travel with crevasse hazards and require proper alpine mountaineering skills. The peak stands at the head of Fairchild Creek with the Fairchild Glacier on its east slope.

set.beta: From the Lower Curtis Glacier, about 600 ft of steep snow in the lower icefall (45 degrees at the top) leads to a large transverse crevasse (crossed on a snow bridge), then a short band of vertical ice in a rock chimney, about 150 ft more steep snow to the top of the icefall, and 60 ft of unprotected 5.0 rock onto the glacier tongue. 100 ft of steep snow leads to a second large transverse crevasse (crossed on the left), then 300 ft of steep ice/snow (60 degrees at the bottom, 70 near the top) to the headwall base. Traverse left at the headwall to a weakness with 100 ft of 4th class to a ledge, traverse left around a corner, then climb ~1,000 ft of easy 5th-class rock on good rock to the crest of the main SE Ridge.

set.rappels: None on the descent - the way off is the South Ridge on foot, which in good conditions takes only about 30 minutes from the summit back to the ridge and basin, far quicker than the ascent. Carry the rappel device and slings on this route's list for RETREAT rather than for the descent: bailing back over the icefall means building your own anchors, and the loose rock above it holds them poorly, so downclimbing carefully or waiting out conditions is usually the better option.

set.approach: Park at the Putvin Trailhead (FST 813, ~1,565 ft) on Hamma Hamma Road (FR 25) — note that in recent years a slide/washout near mile 10.5 has at times blocked the final ~1.2 miles of road, forcing an extra road-walk to the actual trailhead, so check current Forest Service status before you go. From the trailhead the Putvin Trail follows the west side of Boulder Creek for a few hundred feet, then launches into a long, unrelenting climbing traverse to the west — this trail gains nearly 3,000 ft in under 4 miles and does not ease up. Around 1.3 miles it crosses an old logging road (the tread is easy to lose here; look for the trail continuation slightly downhill) and enters the Skokomish Wilderness/Olympic National Park boundary. Around 4,200 ft there is a short but notable headwall/rock step with an old hand-line (or a large exposed tree root used as a handhold) to surmount slick rock — the crux of the trail itself and a common turnaround point for unprepared hikers, especially wet. The maintained tread ends in a basin around 3.9 miles (~4,500 ft, sometimes called Frog/Fawn Pond), where a rougher way-trail continues up steep, rocky terrain to Lake of the Angels (~4,900 ft), reached around 4 miles in. Snow typically lingers on the north-facing basin above Lake of the Angels well into summer (consolidated snow reported from ~4,500 ft on), so an ice axe (and sometimes microspikes/crampons) is worth carrying into early-mid summer. From Lake of the Angels the route leaves any trail and goes cross-country: a boot path climbs a couple of hundred feet of rocky, brushy ground, then traverses up beneath St. Peter's Gate (the pass southeast of the summit) and back west to a notch on Mount Stone's west ridge; from the notch, class 3 scrambling leads a couple of hundred feet to a shallow hanging basin, then continue through talus/boulder terrain toward the summit block. Total one-way distance is about 4.8 miles with roughly 5,053 ft of gain to the 6,618 ft high point. Hazards: reliable water is available along Boulder Creek and at Lake of the Angels but is scarce above the lake; the gully/rib terrain above the lake is loose and route-finding is nontrivial in cloud or fresh snow; the lower trail's root/rock headwall is genuinely exposed when wet.
set.descent_text: Descend by reversing the ascent line — this is a walk-off/downclimb route with no rappelling. The final summit block (roughly 150-200 ft of terrain) is mostly class 3 but includes one well-documented 15-20 ft class 4 step (a shallow crack, often marked by a cairn) that parties downclimb facing in; no fixed rappel anchor has been reported here in any trip account reviewed, so treat this step as a careful downclimb or build a natural (gear/sling-around-block) rappel only if your party is uncomfortable reversing it. From the summit, retrace the class 2-3 talus/boulder terrain back down to the west-ridge notch, reverse the traverse beneath St. Peter's Gate, and return to Lake of the Angels. From the lake, pick the way-trail back down into the basin and rejoin the maintained Putvin Trail, reversing the hand-line/headwall section around 4,200 ft (the single trickiest spot on the descent when wet or in the afternoon sun on lingering snow) and then the long steep 4-mile descent to the trailhead. Parties on this route (rated S5/T5) log around 5.5 hours up and 4 hours down, roughly 10 hours car-to-car with breaks — budget a full day and start early since the lower trail is exposed and hot in the afternoon. A steep mossy/waterfall gully off-route looks like a descent shortcut but is far worse than reversing the ascent line — stick to the known up-track rather than improvising a shortcut.

set.descent_text: The recorded modern practice is to traverse over the summit and descend the East Ridge (Grade II, Class 4), which puts you back on the eastern side of the mountain. That means downclimbing sustained Class 4 loose rock with occasional improvised rappels off slung blocks — carry tat and a few nuts, since there is no fixed gear on either ridge. Reversing the North Ridge and the Nohokomeen Glacier is possible and considerably easier than the East Ridge, but brings the added problem of finding the correct line back down brushy, cliff-banded terrain to the East Bank Trail, which is hard in the dark. Whichever you choose, scout it before you climb and record a GPS track on the way up through the timber; several north-side parties on this mountain have depended on one to get home. The South Face is a third exit but strands you on the opposite side of the peak from any northern camp.

findings.claim: descent_text: reversing the North Ridge 'means the same downclimbing' as the East Ridge

A 2007 party did exactly that: downclimbed the N Ridge through a keyhole and steep snow to the Nohokomeen, then bushwhacked ~4,500 ft to the East Bank trail, with no rappels mentioned. The East Ridge, by contrast, needed belays and has loose rock on its top third. Clause corrected; the brushy route-finding warning is kept.

set.approach: Park at the Panther Creek / East Bank trailhead on SR 20 near milepost 138 (~1,800 ft), 18.5 miles east of Newhalem. Follow the East Bank Trail 2.4 miles west to a multi-way junction, then take the rightmost branch — the old Little Jack Trail, built by the Forest Service in the early 1900s for pack-animal grazing on the mountain's meadows. This climbs steadily to Little Jack at 6.0 miles from the car, gaining roughly 4,800 ft from the junction to the 6,745 ft summit. From Little Jack, continue northeast along the ridge crest to the notch, where the southwest ridge of Jack Mountain proper rises directly ahead; stay on the crest (the standard route instead traverses east from here to the South Face). Water is scarce on the ridge - plan on carrying or on the meadows' seasonal sources. This is the shortest way to the peak, but the Little Jack traverse takes real stamina.
set.descent_text: Downclimb the Class 4 ridge, building rappel anchors on slung blocks where downclimbing is unattractive - there is no fixed gear and no established rappel line, so carry tat and a few nuts. Once back at the notch, reverse the ridge crest to Little Jack, then descend the Little Jack Trail 6.0 miles to the East Bank Trail junction and out to the highway. The descent is long rather than technical, and the sting is that you must regain ground over the ridge crest between the notch and Little Jack on the way home. An alternative exit down the South Face and out over Jerry Lakes to the Canyon Creek Trailhead exists but leaves you at a different trailhead, several road miles from your car.
